title: Tunable Syngas Formation from Electrochemical CO2 Reduction on Copper Nanowire Arrays
abstract: Producing syngas from electrochemical reduction of CO2 by renewable energy offers an opportunity to reduce CO2 emissions and provide chemicals and fuels. Herein, we report the careful manipulation of the reduction treatment to synthesize copper nanowire arrays (Cu NAs). By thermal oxidation, copper oxide nanowires were grown on a Cu mesh. Then, thermal reduction and electrochemical reduction were used to reduce copper oxide to Cu with the morphologic features largely preserved. The derived Cu NAs are cost-effective electrocatalysts capable of reducing CO2 and H2O for tunable syngas production. It is demonstrated that syngas, the mixture of H2 and CO, could be attained with a wide range of compositions (from 1:2 to 3:1) from CO2 reduction and H2O reduction on these Cu NAs in aqueous solutions. In addition, Cu NAs show a high current density, 4 mA/cm, at a low potential, −0.5 V, with a high syngas faradaic efficiency of over 70%. This approach explores a new method that sheds light on tuning the syngas composition from the electrochemical CO2 reduction by Cu-based catalysts.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: CO2 reduction, copper nanowire arrays, syngas, tunable selectivity, electrocatalysis

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
As the result of acceleration of global climate change due to the high atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide (CO2), there is a need to reduce CO2 concentration in the atmosphere.1,2 As a way to mitigate this issue, CO2 hydrogenation to alcohols and hydrocarbons is one of the potential methods, which often requires high temperature and high pressure.3−6 As a cleaner method, electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) to produce fuels and chemicals by renewable energy represents a promising approach.7−9 Over the last decade, the production of CO and HCOOH from ECR has attracted much research interest.10−12
In the same range of potentials as ECR, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) takes place as a competitive reaction.13 Such a scenario has inspired research on the production of syngas (H2 and CO), which can be subsequently upgraded to long-chain hydrocarbons by well-established industrial processes.14−16 For the synthesis of different hydrocarbons, syngas production with controlled H2/CO ratios is needed. Typically, a H2/CO ratio of 2:1 is ideal for methanol production and a H2/CO ratio of 1:1 is desirable for dimethyl ether production,17 whereas Fischer−Tropsch reactors need a H2/CO ratio of 0.6:1.
15 Controlling the reaction rates of ECR and the HER offers an opportunity to produce syngas with tunable composition. Furthermore, the current syngas production is mainly from nonrenewable fossil sources, e.g., coal and natural gas.18 Thus, obtaining syngas mixtures from ECR by renewable energy is a viable option to
achieve the targets of reducing CO2 emissions and moving toward a low-carbon economy. Recently, a number of catalysts, including cadmium sulfoselenide nanorods,16 Cu-enriched Au,15 silver nanowire/ carbon sheet composites,19 and silver diphosphide nanocrystals,20 have been demonstrated as active catalysts for ECR syngas formation. However, ECR technologies are still far from being economically completive. For practical applications, it is essential to prepare earth-abundant-element-based electrocatalysts with the capability of large current density at low overpotential.11 As an earth-abundant element, copper (Cu) is one of the most studied materials for ECR.21−23 However, Cu electrodes normally hold high overpotentials and poor product selectivities for ECR.24 Recently, oxide-derived (OD) Cu catalysts exhibited enhanced performance for ECR.25,26 In the later studies, surface treatments showed an influence on the selectivity and activity of OD-Cu catalysts for ECR.27,28
Compared to bulk materials, nanowires (NWs), onedimensional materials, usually possess higher surface areas leading to higher activity for ECR.25,29 Herein, we report the synthesis of OD-Cu nanowire arrays (NAs) by controlled

Copper oxide (CuOx) NAs were first grown by annealing Cu mesh in air and then were reduced to OD-Cu NAs by employing consecutive thermal and electrochemical reduction. Electrocatalytic studies demonstrate that the composition of syngas can be well-tuned (from 1:2 to 3:1) with high current density at low overpotentials for ECR.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Chemicals. Copper mesh (99.99%, 100 mesh) and carbon dioxide (CO2, 99.999%) were used without purification. Hydrochloric acid (HCl), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.99%), perchloric acid (HClO4, 70%), and an anion exchange membrane were purchased from Shanghai Lingfeng, Macklin, Aladdin (Chinese companies, Shanghai), and Tokuyama (Tokyo, Japan), respectively. The 0.1 mol/L KHCO3 electrolyte solution was prepared using the 18.2 MΩ·cm deionized (DI) H2O. 2.2. Synthesis of NAs. 2.2.1. Growth of CuOx NAs. The Cu mesh was cleaned in 1 mol/L HCl by sonication for 1 min to remove the native oxide layer. It was then rinsed with DI water several times. After drying in N2, the Cu mesh was immediately put in a muffle furnace and annealed in air at 600 °C for 4 h to grow CuOx NAs. 30
2.2.2. Synthesis of OD-Cu NAs. The Cu NAs were synthesized by a two-step method including thermal reduction and electrochemical reduction. First, nonfully reduced CuOx NAs were obtained by annealing the CuOx NAs in forming gas (5% H2/N2, 50 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm)) at 300 °C for approximately 5, 10, and 15 min, respectively. To be noted, fully reduced Cu NAs could be obtained by annealing the CuOx NAs at 300 °C for approximately 45 min in the forming gas. Then, electrochemical reduction at −0.3 V (vs the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)) was used to convert the nonfully reduced CuOx NAs to OD-Cu NAs in N2 purged 0.1 mol/L KHCO3 electrolyte. The electrochemical reduction was monitored by recording the cathodic current. The sign for the complete reduction was that the current reached a near-zero steady state (Figure S1). The total charge passed during the reduction process was recorded as an indication for different types of nonfully reduced CuOx NAs. Thus, the nonfully reduced CuOx NAs in this study could be denoted by a unit: C/cm2 (charge per electrode area). The obtained OD-Cu NAs were used as catalysts for electrochemical CO2 reduction. 2.3. Material Characterizations. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) measurements were performed using an FEI Quanta FEG 250 microscope operated at 30 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected using a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα source (λ = 1.5406 Å). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out with a PHI VersaProbe II spectrometer. All XPS spectra were calibrated to their corresponding C 1 s (284.8 eV). The Cu mesh sample was measured after the HCl acid cleaning treatment to remove the surface oxides. 2.4. Electrochemical Measurements. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was conducted using a CHI workstation (CHI760E, CH Instruments) and a gas-tight closed, two-compartment electrochemical cell (H-type cell) (Figure S2). All the applied potentials were reported vs RHE potentials according to eq 1:
= + + ×E E(vs RHE) (vs Ag/AgCl) 0.199 V 0.0591 V pH (1)
The potentiostat was compensated with 85% of iR values.31 The electrolyte was purged with CO2 at a rate of 30 sccm for 15 min, for the saturation of CO2 in the electrolyte. After CO2 saturation, the pH of the electrolyte was 6.8. The cathode and anode compartments were separated with an anion exchange membrane to reduce the oxidation of the products. An Ag/AgCl placed at the cathode compartment and a piece of Pt plate placed at the anode compartment were used as the reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. CO2 was continuously delivered to the cathode compartment at 10 sccm during the electrolysis. The electrochemical CO2 reduction was carried out in an ambient environment. The gaseous products were
periodically analyzed online by gas chromatography (Ruimin GC2060, Shanghai) approximately every 15 min. CO and H2 from CO2 reduction were detected using a flame ionization detector and thermal conductivity detector, respectively. Argon was used as a carrier gas. The faradaic efficiency (FE) of gaseous products was calculated by eq 2:

The liquid products produced during the reaction were analyzed using a Bruker Avance 400 M nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer. The electrolyte was added with D2O to form a (90:10) % volume-ratio solution with a known concentration of an internal standard (dimethyl sulfoxide). 2.5. Determination of Electrochemical Active Surface Area. The surface roughness factor and electrochemical active surface area were evaluated by double-layer capacitance that can be obtained by recording cyclic voltammograms (CVs) in 0.1 mol/L HClO4 at various scan rates. CV measurement was conducted in the same electrochemical cell after the CuOx NAs were electrochemically reduced at −0.3 V vs RHE. A potential window from 0−0.2 V was carried out in a non-Faradaic potential region, and the current density was plotted vs the scan rate of CVs. The capacitance of the electrode could be determined using the slope.25

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Figure 1a demonstrates the synthesis process of OD-Cu NAs on a Cu mesh via a three-step method, which includes thermal
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01504 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
oxidation, thermal reduction, and electrochemical reduction. Briefly, CuOx NAs were first synthesized by annealing the Cu mesh at 600 °C in air. Then, the thermal reduction of CuOx NAs was performed at 300 °C in forming gas (5% H2/N2). By controlling the thermal reduction time, CuOx NAs with various reduction levels could be synthesized. The nonfully reduced CuOx NAs were denoted as a unit of C/cm
2 (the amount of charge passed per electrode area in the electrochemical reduction, σ). Thus, the surface charge density (σ) required to reduce the CuOx could be related to the amounts of CuOx on the NA surface. For instance, CuOx NAs-42 C/cm 2 represents the CuOx NAs with σ = 42 C/cm 2, as shown in Figure 1a. Last, the various levels of nonfully reduced CuOx NAs were fully reduced to OD-Cu NAs by applying a negative potential in 0.1 mol/L KHCO3. Detailed information on the synthesis process is in the Experimental Section. The representative SEM images of the Cu mesh, assynthesized CuOx NAs, and CuOx NAs-42 C/cm 2 are shown in Figure 1b−d. From the images, the CuOx NWs were mainly grown vertically to the Cu mesh surface. The diameters of the obtained CuOx NWs were in the range of 50−100 nm, while the lengths could be tens of μm. Figure 1e shows representative SEM images of OD-Cu NAs that were generated from CuOx NAs-42 C/cm
2. According to these images, the OD-Cu NAs preserved the general dimensions of the CuOx NAs, despite some impairment of tips of the original NAs. Figures S3−S5 demonstrate similar dimensions and morphology of OD-Cu NAs generated from other CuOx NAs with different reduction levels (i.e., σ = 15, 25, and 57 C/cm2). Following the minor morphological change of Cu NAs
during the oxidation and reduction processes, we sought to determine the structural and chemical evolution of the NAs using XRD and XPS. Figure 2a shows the XRD patterns of the Cu mesh, CuOx NAs-42 C/cm
2, and OD-Cu NAs. On comparing the XRD patterns of the Cu mesh and CuOx NAs, it is seen that both samples have intense diffraction peaks at 2θ values of 43.4, 50.4, and 74.1° (Figure 2a), which is characteristic of the cubic Cu. Evidently, the XRD pattern of CuOx NAs shows additional diffraction peaks associated with crystalline Cu2O and CuO for 2θ ranging between 35 and 75°. The XRD pattern of the OD-Cu NAs presents the same peaks of cubic Cu as the Cu mesh, despite a weak Cu2O peak at 36− 37o. This small amount of Cu2O may suggest that some grain boundaries (GBs) exist in the OD-Cu NAs because GBs can promote the re-oxidation of Cu.28,34 The substantial change in
the XRD patterns indicated that CuOx NAs-42 C/cm 2 is composed of a mixture of metallic Cu, Cu2O, and CuO, while the OD-Cu NAs consist mainly of metallic Cu. Similar XRD patterns were observed for other levels of nonfully reduced CuOx NAs (i.e., σ = 15, 25, and 57 C/cm
2) and accordingly electrochemically reduced OD-Cu NAs, as shown in Figures S6 and S7. Figure 2b,c shows the Cu 2p and Cu LMM photoelectron spectra of the Cu mesh, CuOx NAs-42 C/cm 2, and OD-Cu NAs. The Cu 2p spectrum for CuOx NAs-42 C/cm 2 exhibits two dominating peaks at 932.3 and 952.2 eV of 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 components, respectively, accompanied by their corresponding satellite peaks from 938 to 946 eV. Two major peaks associated with the satellite peaks indicate the existence of Cu2+ in the sample.35 Another nonfully reduced CuOx NAs (σ = 15 C/cm
2) and their electro-reduced OD-Cu NAs exhibit similar XPS spectra, as seen in Figure S8. In contrast, the XPS spectra of the Cu mesh and OD-Cu NAs exhibit the presence of Cu0 peaks at binding energies of 932.3 and 952.2 eV in the absence of satellite peaks. It is worth mentioning that peaks corresponding to Cu0 and Cu+ have the same binding energies.36,37 Thus, subsequent Cu Auger LMM spectra were recorded to further determine the chemical state of Cu (Figure 2c). The Cu mesh only exhibits a single peak of Cu0 at 567.9 eV, while OD-Cu NAs present characteristic peaks of Cu0 and Cu+ at 567.9 and 569.9 eV.38 For CuOx NAs42 C/cm2, a characteristic peak of Cu2+ can be seen at 568.7 eV. Combining Cu 2p and LMM spectra, we conclude that the majority of Cu in the Cu mesh exists as Cu0, while that in ODCu NAs is in the form of Cu+ and Cu0. Although the XPS data demonstrated the co-existence of Cu+ and Cu0 in OD-Cu NAs, the XRD pattern of this sample was indicative of the cubic Cu0
structure (Figure 2b,c). This observation implies that the oxidation of Cu may take place only at the surface because the XPS technique primarily probes the NA surface. The electrochemical studies of CO2 reduction were performed using the OD-Cu NAs as electrocatalysts. The CO2 reduction on the OD-Cu NAs was measured at −0.45, −0.50, and − 0.55 V vs RHE (all potentials reported in this work are referred to the RHE reference) in 0.1 mol/L KHCO3 electrolyte in the ambient environment for several hours. These potentials were carefully selected to avoid large experimental errors for low current densities (i.e., > − 0.45 V) or the mass transport limitations (i.e., < −0.55 V).26 These experiments were carried out in an H-type cell that consists of
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01504 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
two compartments, separated with an anion-exchange membrane. Details of the electrochemical measurements can be found in the Experimental Section. As shown in Figures S9−S12, the OD-Cu NAs presented a current density of ∼4 mA/cm2 under low potential (−0.50 V). This value was higher than the reported current densities of Ag NW and Au-Cu NW catalysts (see SI Table S1 for the catalytic performance of various catalysts).39,40 Additionally, the OD-Cu NAs exhibited great stability over 10 hours under reaction conditions (Figure S13). Figure 3a−c shows the FE of CO and H2 as a function of σ at different potentials. It is noted that H2 was produced during electrolysis because the HER was accompanied by CO2 reduction.
13 The Cu active sites can be occupied/reacted by both H2O and CO2 molecules, and thus the reaction of an individual gas is likely inhibited by another gas, resulting in different HER and ECR reaction rates. At all studied potentials, the FE for H2 production decreased and that for CO production increased with the increasing σ. To determine the composition of the synthesized syngas, the ratio of H2 and CO FEs is compared for all OD-Cu NAs, as shown in Figure 3d. Despite the Cu NAs with the smallest σ, the H2/CO ratio can be regulated to match the syngas
compositions for the Fischer−Tropsch synthesis of hydrocarbons (H2/CO = 0.6:1), dimethyl ether synthesis (H2/CO = 1:1), and methanol production (H2/CO = 2:1).
41 In the optimal syngas region, the OD-Cu NAs catalyzed ECR to syngas with a total FE of over 70% at −0.50 V. Additional FEs of liquid products are shown in Figure S14. Even though FE is good for reporting the selectivity of
catalysts, it may not present the true difference with respect to catalytic activity among all catalysts studied.42 Instead, the measurement of partial current densities for CO and H2 is a better descriptor to determine the different activities among various OD-NAs.42 Figure 4 summarizes the comparison of the partial current densities among these OD-Cu NAs. Generally, the H2 production rate decreased distinctly with a larger σ. In contrast, the CO production rate increased in the same experimental settings. For instance, the rate of the HER decreased from 2.7 to 1.0 mA/cm2, whereas the rate of CO production increased from 0.8 to 1.8 mA/cm2 at −0.50 V (Figure 4b). To investigate the intrinsic activity of the OD-Cu NAs,
reaction activity was normalized by the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA). Thus, the ECSA of the OD-Cu NAs was
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01504 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
determined by measuring the double-layer capacitance. The capacitance was 10.1, 13.2, 13.0, and 16.7 mF/cm2 for the ODCu NAs in an σ-increased order (Figures S15 and S16). It has been reported that the enhanced capacitance is attributed to an increase in the surface roughness of the catalyst.26,43 Thus, surface features of the NAs can be tuned by modulating the oxidation and reduction conditions. The ECSA normalized activities for H2 and CO observed on various OD-Cu NAs are shown in Figure 5. It is noted that the normalized H2 and CO activities exhibit similar trends to those before normalization over the studied range of σ. For example, the rate of the HER decreased from 0.26 to 0.06 mA/cm2, whereas the rate of CO production only increased from 0.08 to 0.11 mA/cm2 at −0.50 V (Figure 5b). To further understand the change of intrinsic catalytic
performance, electrocatalytic measurements of the HER on various OD-Cu NAs were performed (Figures S17−S23). The OD-Cu NAs exhibited a unity FE for the HER. The ECSA normalized H2 activity observed on various OD-Cu NAs as
ECR is shown in Figure 6a. The normalized H2 activity increased first and then decreased distinctly when the σ grew larger. Considering that ECR and HER are two competing reactions on the cathode, the decrease in H2 selectivity is because of the improvement of ECR activity, as displayed in Figures 4 and 5. Based on a previous report, the reaction activity and
selectivity of the OD-Cu catalysts showed a dependence on the initial thickness of the Cu2O layer.
26 In the following studies, the enhanced catalytic performance of OD-materials was attributed to the GBs.44,45 These GBs could be created by employing electrochemical reduction treatment on the CuOx species.34 Therefore, the thermal and electrochemical reduction treatment in our experiments plays an important role in inducing GBs in OD-Cu NA catalysts, which in turn has a profound impact on the resultant catalytic activities. It has also been demonstrated that GB surface terminations are active for ECR but not for the HER,46 since lattice strain induced by GBs could tune the binding energies for CO2 reduction
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c01504 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
intermediates and thus reduces the CO2 activation barriers. Hence, the reaction rates of ECR and the HER can be finetuned by optimizing the GB density by systematically applying different reduction treatments, as illustrated in Figure 6c. With the increasing density of GBs, the catalysts display high activity in ECR but low activity in the HER, producing syngas with a low H2/CO ratio (Figures 3−6). To obtain insights into the mechanism of CO2 reduction on the OD-Cu NAs, Tafel slopes for CO production are shown in Figure 6b. In the range of overpotential (0.09−0.29 V), these plots are linear with a slope of 117, 121, 116, and 121 mV/ decade, respectively. The slopes are consistent with an initial electron transfer to CO2, forming a CO2
•‑ intermediate on the surface of the electrode as the rate-determining step.47

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we have synthesized dense OD-Cu NAs as efficient catalysts for ECR via a three-step method. First, CuOx NAs were grown on the Cu mesh by thermal oxidation, then the CuOx NAs were reduced by annealing in forming gas, and finally, the nonfully reduced CuOx NAs were reduced to ODCu NAs by applying a cathodic potential. The OD-Cu NAs largely maintained the original morphology of the CuOx NAs. Studies of ECR showed that these OD-Cu NAs could produce syngas compositions with a wide range (from 1:2 to 3:1) at high production rates with low overpotentials. To be specific, the FE and current densities of CO production increased with the current densities of the HER decreased when the σ of CuOx NAs grew larger at applied potentials. The reason could be attributed to the GBs created by the electrochemical reduction treatment. Mechanistic studies indicated that all OD-Cu NAs possessed the same rate-determining initial electron transfer. This work brings an opportunity to develop carbon-neutral syngas production from ECR by Cu-based catalysts. In addition, this synthetic approach may provide an effective method for tuning the selectivity of the OD-Cu catalyst for ECR.
